reviews.review: Addictive

A masterclass in managing chaos. Darkest Dungeon is easily one of the most stressful experiences you can have in gaming, yet it is equally rewarding. At its core, this game isn't about being an all-powerful hero; it’s about learning how to make the absolute best out of a terrible situation.
Uniquely, playing this game taught me a lot about managing my own emotions in the face of tragedy. It forces you to expect things to go wrong. It taught me to simply focus on doing the best within my power, maintaining my mental fortitude, and keeping my resolution intact even when everything is crumbling.
To top it all off, the Ancestor is arguably the greatest narrator to ever be born in video game history. His voice perfectly punctuates your highest triumphs and your deepest downfalls. If you want a game that tests your mind as much as your strategic skills, this is it.

You WILL suffer. You WILL fail in your expeditions. You WILL watch your favorite character die because they got targeted by all enemies at once without a chance to heal. You WILL scream in excitement when you finally get a virtue against the boss that saves the entire run. You WILL find your first ever secret room after 50 weeks after you forgot to bring a key with you. And you WILL ragequit at week 90 after getting party-wiped in your first Darkest Dungeon expedition after putting 50 hours into your save. You WILL learn from this mistake and not learn overconfidence, this insidious and slow killer, overwhelm you.

In time, you will learn the tragic extents of your failings, and adapt (all that for a skewer to kill 2 of your characters in a single hit) and YOU. WILL. ENJOY. IT

I can't believe how many years I have gone without leaving a review on this piece of art --today, I will remedy that. 

I don't know how to explain Darkest Dungeon to you. This is simply one of the best games I have ever played. It literally is it's own genre. It's unlike anything else I have seen before. And I have seen nothing else like it since then.

The atmosphere this game has is unique, you totally feel drawn in to the world even though it's mostly 2D sprites on a screen. I think the narrator plays a big part in it. Even though it's in a dark fantasy setting, being in the Hamlet gives me a unique joy and comfort and a sense of "being home". This is the closest I have felt this way since being in Rogue Encampment in Diablo II. And I am certain I have a lot of positive bias towards D2, which probably makes this an even bigger achievement for Darkest Dungeon.

So, let me say a few things about the gameplay. This game teaches you humility. It is not for the faint of heart. It is not for narcissists who blame others for their mistakes. It is not for people who shy away from a challenge, nor for people who avoid responsibility. This game punishes hubris, greed, and overconfidence. There is a reason the ancestor repeatedly says:

"Overconfidence is a slow but insidious killer."

Because that literally is the premise of Darkest Dungeon. It is the root cause behind the lore. It is the definition of the core gameplay loop. I have no clue how they managed to implement something so perfect, so fitting. This is literally a piece of art. If you can not appreciate this I don't think we could see eye to eye about the depth of things in life. 

It's a unique game that will always hold a special place in my life and one that I will always keep coming back to every few years because to me it will never grow old. It just ages like fine wine.

Also, if you would like to experience the true Darkest Dungeon, play on Bloodmoon. If you can still keep your wits about you, then you are a true challenger of life to behold.

"The way is lit. The path is clear. We require only the strength to follow it."

I understand the appeal. Definitely a must try for anyone that loves turn-based combat and dark fantasy. Replayability wise in my opinion slightly lacking, The early levels become extremely repetitive that you just want to get on with them and do the final bosses to continue onto the darkest dungeon itself.
In terms of characters there is a lot that this game does well and a lot that is extremely lacking. It suffers from what a lot of roguelites suffer from which is repetitive buildpatterns and gameplay loop that gets boring. Builds can be very varied at the start but you tend to neglect most of it as you progress and do basic dungeon diving and only leave specific builds for bosses. In terms of relics and upgrades, they are fine but there isn't much variety.
What got me interested was definitely the final dungeon, side content (including DLC's) and the bosses.
It offers high stakes and a lot of challenge (in terms of game knowledge), the added stress meter allows for a double edged sword style of gameplay which i enjoy quite a bit.
Overall its a game meant to be played multiple times but fails to make the gameplay engaging enough to keep me coming back to it. You either play extremely passively, making this more of a walking sim than a dark fantasy dungeon crawler, or you play extremely aggressive and watch as your party dies over and over again.
Definitely recommended as a first timer, but be prepared for a lot of challenges that make you want to tear your hair out.

Best dungeon crawler ive ever played. It was genuine fun. Im not a huge fun of turn based games, but on this game it was executed so well, each character having their own position in the party that fits their skill sets. Not to mention you can play a single character 2 different ways with how flexible their skill sets are.

Having to manage not just health but also sanity was also a great feature that made sure you get punished if you get careless, having to decide whether to kill the damage dealer or the one that spits on your party slowly filling the sanity bar.
Equipment you get is great and a huge tide turner if the right ones are used on the right mercs,
Boss fights are great and each having their own unique moveset or gimmick.
The areas that are separated having their own separate enemies with different weakness encourages to try out different mercs, and actually needed you to keep an eye out for their traits.
Plot twist was great, might come as a shock to some people.

ALSO, NARRATOR IS SO GOOOOOOOOOOOD.

Not to mention the mods in this game are great, the classes and quality of life mods fit perfectly for the game.

By all means, this game gets worse the more experienced you are with it. At the start you will have the thrills of fighting scary intese fights against unknown new enemies and new areas, trying new strategies and all of that. But eventually you will discover what works best in each area and the gameplay crumbles down to risk minimizing procedures that starts right from team composition before any fight happens.
The game actively combats player creativity and self-expression, because both do not minimize risks and the potential loss is far too great to justify deviating from the "procedure".

One good thing about the game is the mod support and the current mod content, but I'd argue that only new classes mods are benefitial for the game. Enemy mods, specially ones that add new enemy to pre-existing areas (like the Crimson Court dlc), has the potential to only harm the gameplay. For example: the Crimson Courd dlc itself that adds high priority blight resistant enemies to all dungeons (if you happen to release them from the garden) it ends up filtering out blight strategies from "blight weak locations", because to minimize risks your team must be effective against ALL possible scenarios in a given location and that mantra must triumph over the entire gameplay. If you add too many enemies not "designed for the location" eventually all of your teams will devolve to triple Shieldbreaker + Vestal (which is not a great team, but if you consider all possible fights at once this team is the best "in average" and the average is what you seek).

It is so funny that the best strategy against the Crimson Court dlc is to simply not engage it (once it appears around week 4) until you can one-shot all main missions of all levels in a row (because once you do the enemies stop appearing in all locations, therefore correcting the bad design).

After playing it for so long you will understand that the game is repetitive and strategically shallow. So if you buy it cherish your lack of understanding for as long as you can and quit it once you discover the "procedure".

I hate to have to suddenly criticize a game that I have thoroughly enjoyed over the years but not only the Butcher's Circus icon in the Hamlet sticks out like a sore thumb, it also partially covers the stagecoach's clickbox so I couldn't ignore it even if I wanted to. I tried to, but then came the BC town events that I welcomed with the same tired sigh I reserve to capchas and intrusive ads. ːblightː

While It's great the devs still take the time to expand the scope of DD, I'm not interested in PVP activities and this is not what I purchased Darkest Dungeon for, quite the contrary. The worst is that you can't disable that DLC and I feel this is a weird departure from letting people enable and disable DLCs at will... why suddenly change something which worked? 

I wish the PVP content was entirely self-contained instead of having it bleed over to my solo campaign in an intrusive way. I noticed mods disabling the BC elements but I'd rather have the official option to keep playing the vanilla game if possible. Alternatively, I feel the Butcher's Circus elements like the banner could be at the very least integrated a little better into the hamlet screen.

I'm afraid adding unfinished content - Fire's Edge DLC - to advertise the sequel is only going to make me more annoyed about that forceful way of doing marketing. Get the hint, guys.

After witnessing horrors unfathomable and indescribable from beyond, please be sure to keep company, get drunk and gamble your life savings so you can return to grueling walking in a singular direction to retrieve loot for some dead guy's infinitely more intelligent and better looking relative. 

Also you may be The Flame, but its light pales in comparison to the gleaming treasure you'll find while banging into every wall in pitch-blackness.

Just don't get shuffled around too much *wink wink*

To enjoy this game, one must embrace hardship and roll with the punches. You must be able to understand risks and plans and operate despite them. You must embrace the difficulties, and use it as a way to become better.
This game is amazing. Hands down. It's difficult and heartbreaking, but the victories make it feel that much sweeter.
